questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Provisions applicable in the absence of a partnership deed
questions.question: In the absence of a partnership deed, a partner who has advanced a loan to the firm is entitled to interest on it at:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 6% p.a.
Why: When there is no deed, Section 13(d) of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 applies — a partner's loan (an advance over and above his capital) carries interest at 6% p.a. It is a charge against profit, so it is payable even if the firm incurs a loss.
Why not the others:
(A) 12% p.a. would apply only if the partners had agreed on it in a deed.
(C) The Act prescribes no 9% rate.
(D) 'No interest' is the rule for interest on capital, not for a partner's loan.
Key point: No deed → profits shared equally, no interest on capital, no salary or commission, but 6% p.a. interest on partners' loans.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.question: A partner withdrew ₹6,000 at the end of every month during the year ended 31 March 2026. Interest on drawings is charged at 10% p.a. The interest on drawings will be:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹3,300
Given: ₹6,000 withdrawn at the END of each month for 12 months; rate 10% p.a.
Formula: Interest = Total drawings × Rate × Average period ÷ 12. For equal monthly drawings at the end of each month, average period = (11 + 0) ÷ 2 = 5.5 months.
Step 1: Total drawings = ₹6,000 × 12 = ₹72,000
Step 2: Interest = ₹72,000 × 10/100 × 5.5/12 = ₹3,300
Common mistake: Taking 6 months (drawings in the middle of the month) gives ₹3,600 (A); 6.5 months (beginning of the month) gives ₹3,900 (B); charging interest for the full year gives ₹7,200 (D).

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Guarantee of profit to a partner
questions.question: A, B and C are partners sharing profits in the ratio 3 : 2 : 1. C is guaranteed a minimum profit of ₹40,000 and any deficiency is to be borne by A alone. The firm's profit for the year is ₹1,80,000. A's share of profit will be:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹80,000
Given: Ratio 3 : 2 : 1; profit ₹1,80,000; C guaranteed ₹40,000; deficiency borne by A only.
Step 1: C's normal share = ₹1,80,000 × 1/6 = ₹30,000
Step 2: Deficiency = ₹40,000 − ₹30,000 = ₹10,000
Step 3: A's normal share = ₹1,80,000 × 3/6 = ₹90,000; after bearing the deficiency = ₹90,000 − ₹10,000 = ₹80,000 (B gets ₹60,000 and C gets ₹40,000; total ₹1,80,000).
Common mistake: Ignoring the guarantee gives ₹90,000 (B); sharing the deficiency between A and B in 3 : 2 gives ₹84,000 (C); deducting the entire guaranteed amount from A gives ₹50,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account of a partnership firm:
(A) Interest on partners' capital is debited to it.
(B) Interest on a partner's loan is debited to it.
(C) Interest on partners' drawings is credited to it.
(D) Rent paid to a partner for the firm's use of his building is debited to it.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A) and (C) only
Why: The Appropriation Account shows how profit is divided among partners. Items that are appropriations of profit — interest on capital (debit), interest on drawings (credit), salary or commission to partners (debit) — go here.
Why not the others:
(A) and (C) of the options include statement (B) or (D) — but interest on a partner's loan and rent paid to a partner are charges against profit. They are debited to the Profit and Loss Account, not the Appropriation Account, because they are payable whether or not the firm earns a profit.
(B) contains only the two incorrect statements.
Key point: Charge against profit (loan interest, rent to partner) → P&L Account; appropriation of profit (interest on capital, salary, commission, interest on drawings) → P&L Appropriation Account.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.question: When partners' capitals are fixed, a partner's share of profit, salary and interest on capital are credited to his:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Current Account
Why: Under the fixed capital method each partner has two accounts. The Capital Account records only the original capital (and any additional capital or permanent withdrawal). All regular adjustments — share of profit, salary, commission, interest on capital, drawings and interest on drawings — are recorded in the Current Account.
Why not the others:
(A) Crediting the Capital Account is the fluctuating capital method.
(C) A Loan Account records a partner's loan to the firm, not his share of profit.
(D) The Drawings Account records withdrawals and is closed to the Current Account.
Key point: Fixed capital → two accounts per partner (Capital + Current); fluctuating capital → one account.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.question: X and Y share profits equally. Their fixed capitals are ₹3,00,000 and ₹2,00,000. After the accounts for the year were closed, it was found that interest on capital at 10% p.a., as provided in the deed, had been omitted. The single adjusting entry will be:
options: A) Y's Current A/c Dr. ₹5,000; To X's Current A/c ₹5,000
B) X's Current A/c Dr. ₹5,000; To Y's Current A/c ₹5,000
C) Y's Current A/c Dr. ₹20,000; To X's Current A/c ₹20,000
D) P&L Adjustment A/c Dr. ₹50,000; To X's and Y's Current A/cs ₹50,000
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Y's Current A/c Dr. ₹5,000; To X's Current A/c ₹5,000
Given: Capitals X ₹3,00,000, Y ₹2,00,000; ratio 1 : 1; omitted interest on capital @ 10% p.a.
Step 1: Interest that should have been credited: X ₹30,000; Y ₹20,000; total ₹50,000
Step 2: The same ₹50,000 was wrongly distributed as profit, so it must be taken back in the profit ratio 1 : 1: X ₹25,000; Y ₹25,000
Step 3: Net effect: X = +₹30,000 − ₹25,000 = +₹5,000 (credit); Y = +₹20,000 − ₹25,000 = −₹5,000 (debit)
Step 4: Single entry: Y's Current A/c Dr. ₹5,000; To X's Current A/c ₹5,000
Common mistake: Reversing the direction gives (B); using only Y's interest of ₹20,000 gives (C); (D) records the interest but forgets to take back the profit already distributed.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Division of profit in the absence of a deed
questions.question:
Assertion (A): In the absence of a partnership deed, profits are shared equally among the partners.
Reason (R): In the absence of a partnership deed, profits are shared in the ratio of the partners' capitals.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
Why: Section 13(b) of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 says that, unless otherwise agreed, partners share profits and losses equally — so the Assertion is true. The Reason is false: the amount of capital contributed has no bearing on the profit-sharing ratio when there is no deed.
Why not the others:
(A) and (B) need the Reason to be true, which it is not.
(D) The Assertion is a correct statement of the law.
Key point: No deed → equal sharing, regardless of unequal capitals.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.question: Ravi, a partner, is entitled to a commission of 10% of the net profit after charging such commission. The net profit before charging the commission is ₹2,20,000. Ravi's commission is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹20,000
Given: Net profit before commission ₹2,20,000; commission 10% of profit AFTER charging the commission.
Formula: Commission = Profit before commission × Rate ÷ (100 + Rate)
Step 1: Commission = ₹2,20,000 × 10/110 = ₹20,000
Step 2: Check: profit after commission = ₹2,00,000, and 10% of ₹2,00,000 = ₹20,000 ✔
Common mistake: Taking 10% of the profit before commission gives ₹22,000 (A); using 110/100 instead of 10/110 gives ₹24,200 (B); deducting 10% twice gives ₹18,000 (C).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Change in profit-sharing ratio — sacrificing and gaining ratio
questions.question: A and B share profits in the ratio 5 : 3. From 1 April 2026 they decide to share profits equally. Which of the following correctly describes the change?
options: A) A sacrifices 1/8 and B gains 1/8
B) B sacrifices 1/8 and A gains 1/8
C) A sacrifices 1/2 and B gains 1/2
D) Neither partner sacrifices, as the total share remains the same
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) A sacrifices 1/8 and B gains 1/8
Given: Old ratio 5 : 3 (5/8, 3/8); new ratio 1 : 1 (4/8, 4/8).
Formula: Sacrifice (or gain) = Old share − New share. A positive result is a sacrifice; a negative result is a gain.
Step 1: A = 5/8 − 4/8 = 1/8 → sacrifice
Step 2: B = 3/8 − 4/8 = −1/8 → gain of 1/8
Common mistake: Using New − Old reverses the result (B); comparing the new share itself (1/2) with nothing gives (C); (D) confuses the unchanged total (1) with the change in individual shares.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Admission of a partner — new profit-sharing ratio
questions.question: A and B share profits in the ratio 3 : 2. They admit C for a 1/5th share, which he acquires equally from A and B. The new profit-sharing ratio of A, B and C will be:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 5 : 3 : 2
Given: Old ratio 3 : 2; C gets 1/5, taken EQUALLY from A and B (1/10 each).
Step 1: A's new share = 3/5 − 1/10 = 6/10 − 1/10 = 5/10
Step 2: B's new share = 2/5 − 1/10 = 4/10 − 1/10 = 3/10
Step 3: C's share = 1/5 = 2/10
Step 4: New ratio = 5 : 3 : 2
Common mistake: If C took his share from A and B in their old ratio, the answer would be 12 : 8 : 5 (B). (A) simply adds C at 1 without calculating; (D) gives C a share of 1/5 but splits the rest equally.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.question: The profits of a firm for the last four years were: 2021-22 ₹80,000; 2022-23 ₹1,00,000; 2023-24 a loss of ₹20,000; 2024-25 ₹1,20,000. Goodwill is to be valued at two years' purchase of the average profit of these four years. The value of goodwill is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹1,40,000
Given: Profits ₹80,000, ₹1,00,000, (₹20,000) loss, ₹1,20,000; 2 years' purchase.
Formula: Goodwill = Average profit × Number of years' purchase
Step 1: Total profit = 80,000 + 1,00,000 − 20,000 + 1,20,000 = ₹2,80,000
Step 2: Average profit = ₹2,80,000 ÷ 4 = ₹70,000
Step 3: Goodwill = ₹70,000 × 2 = ₹1,40,000
Common mistake: Adding the loss instead of deducting it gives an average of ₹80,000 and goodwill of ₹1,60,000 (A). ₹2,80,000 (C) is the total profit, and ₹70,000 (D) is the average profit — neither has been multiplied by the years' purchase.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Goodwill — capitalisation of average profit method
questions.question: A firm earns an average profit of ₹80,000. The normal rate of return in the industry is 10%. The firm's total assets are ₹6,50,000 and its outside liabilities are ₹1,00,000. The value of goodwill by the capitalisation of average profit method is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹2,50,000
Given: Average profit ₹80,000; normal rate 10%; total assets ₹6,50,000; outside liabilities ₹1,00,000.
Formula: Goodwill = Capitalised value of average profit − Net assets (capital employed)
Step 1: Capitalised value = ₹80,000 × 100/10 = ₹8,00,000
Step 2: Net assets = ₹6,50,000 − ₹1,00,000 = ₹5,50,000
Step 3: Goodwill = ₹8,00,000 − ₹5,50,000 = ₹2,50,000
Common mistake: Forgetting to deduct outside liabilities gives ₹8,00,000 − ₹6,50,000 = ₹1,50,000 (A). (C) is the capitalised value itself. (B) would require net assets of ₹5,00,000, which the data does not give.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Item)
(A) Profit on revaluation at the time of admission
(B) Premium for goodwill brought in by the incoming partner
(C) Retiring partner's share of goodwill
(D) Profit of the reconstituted firm after admission

List-II (Ratio in which it is shared or debited)
(I) Gaining ratio
(II) New profit-sharing ratio
(III) Old profit-sharing ratio
(IV) Sacrificing ratio

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Why:
(A) Revaluation profit belongs to the period before admission, so it goes to the old partners in the OLD ratio → (III).
(B) Goodwill premium compensates the old partners for the share they give up, so it is credited in the SACRIFICING ratio → (IV).
(C) On retirement, the continuing partners who gain the retiring partner's share pay for it in the GAINING ratio → (I).
(D) After admission, profits are shared in the NEW ratio → (II).
Why not the others: (B) swaps old and sacrificing ratios; (C) swaps sacrificing and gaining ratios; (D) applies the new ratio to revaluation profit.
Key point: Before the change → old ratio; compensation on admission → sacrificing ratio; compensation on retirement → gaining ratio; after the change → new ratio.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Revaluation of assets and reassessment of liabilities
questions.question: Which of the following is credited to the Revaluation Account at the time of reconstitution of a partnership firm?
options: A) Decrease in the value of assets
B) Increase in the value of assets
C) Increase in the amount of liabilities
D) Recording of an unrecorded liability
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Increase in the value of assets
Why: The Revaluation Account is credited with gains — an increase in the value of assets or a decrease in liabilities — and debited with losses.
Why not the others:
(A) A fall in asset value is a loss, so it is debited.
(C) A rise in liabilities is a loss, so it is debited.
(D) An unrecorded liability increases what the firm owes, so it is also a loss (debit).
Key point: Gains (assets ↑, liabilities ↓) → credit; losses (assets ↓, liabilities ↑) → debit.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.question: On the admission of a new partner: machinery (book value ₹2,00,000) is revalued at ₹1,80,000; stock is appreciated by ₹15,000; a provision for doubtful debts of ₹4,000 is created; and an unrecorded creditor of ₹6,000 is to be brought into the books. The result of revaluation is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Loss ₹15,000
Given: Machinery −₹20,000; stock +₹15,000; provision for doubtful debts −₹4,000; unrecorded creditor −₹6,000.
Step 1: Losses (debit side) = 20,000 + 4,000 + 6,000 = ₹30,000
Step 2: Gains (credit side) = ₹15,000
Step 3: Net result = ₹15,000 − ₹30,000 = loss of ₹15,000, shared by the old partners in the old ratio.
Common mistake: Treating the unrecorded creditor as a gain gives a loss of ₹3,000 (B); treating both the provision and the creditor as gains gives a profit of ₹5,000 (A); treating the stock appreciation as a loss gives a loss of ₹45,000 (C).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.question: A and B share profits in the ratio 2 : 1 and their capitals, after all adjustments, are ₹1,00,000 and ₹80,000. C is admitted for a 1/4th share in profits and brings ₹1,00,000 as capital, but no separate premium for goodwill. The firm's hidden goodwill is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹1,20,000
Given: C brings ₹1,00,000 for a 1/4 share; old partners' adjusted capitals total ₹1,80,000.
Formula: Hidden goodwill = Implied total capital of the new firm − Actual total capital of all partners
Step 1: Implied total capital = ₹1,00,000 × 4/1 = ₹4,00,000
Step 2: Actual total capital = ₹1,00,000 + ₹80,000 + ₹1,00,000 = ₹2,80,000
Step 3: Hidden goodwill = ₹4,00,000 − ₹2,80,000 = ₹1,20,000
Common mistake: Leaving out C's own capital gives ₹2,20,000 (A). ₹30,000 (B) is C's 1/4 share of the goodwill, not the firm's goodwill. ₹1,00,000 (D) is C's capital.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding the retirement of a partner:
(A) If the amount due to the retiring partner is not paid immediately, it is transferred to his Loan Account.
(B) Gaining ratio = New ratio − Old ratio.
(C) The retiring partner's share of goodwill is debited to the continuing partners in their gaining ratio.
(D) Profit on revaluation at the time of retirement is credited only to the continuing partners, in their new ratio.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why:
(A) True — an unpaid balance becomes a liability of the firm and is shown in the retiring partner's Loan Account.
(B) True — each continuing partner's gain is the excess of his new share over his old share.
(C) True — the partners who gain the retiring partner's share compensate him in the gaining ratio.
(D) False — revaluation profit relates to the period up to retirement, so it is shared by ALL partners, including the retiring partner, in the OLD ratio.
Why not the others: (B) and (C) of the options include the false statement (D); option (D) includes it too.
Key point: Revaluation result and accumulated reserves always go to all old partners in the old ratio.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Retirement — new ratio of continuing partners
questions.question: A, B and C share profits in the ratio 5 : 3 : 2. B retires and his share is taken over by A and C in the ratio 2 : 1. The new profit-sharing ratio of A and C will be:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 7 : 3
Given: Old ratio 5 : 3 : 2; B's share 3/10 is taken by A and C in 2 : 1.
Step 1: A's gain = 3/10 × 2/3 = 2/10; C's gain = 3/10 × 1/3 = 1/10
Step 2: A's new share = 5/10 + 2/10 = 7/10
Step 3: C's new share = 2/10 + 1/10 = 3/10
Step 4: New ratio of A : C = 7 : 3
Common mistake: Just deleting B and keeping A and C's old ratio gives 5 : 2 (A). 2 : 1 (C) is the gaining ratio, not the new ratio. Splitting B's share in the reverse ratio 1 : 2 gives 6/10 and 4/10 = 3 : 2 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Death of a partner — share of profit till the date of death
questions.question: P, Q and R share profits in the ratio 2 : 1 : 1. R died on 30 June 2025. The deed provides that a deceased partner's share of profit till the date of death is to be calculated on the basis of the previous year's profit, which was ₹2,40,000. The firm closes its books on 31 March every year. R's share of profit till the date of death is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹15,000
Given: Previous year's profit ₹2,40,000; R's share 1/4; period 1 April to 30 June 2025 = 3 months.
Step 1: Profit for 3 months on time basis = ₹2,40,000 × 3/12 = ₹60,000
Step 2: R's share = ₹60,000 × 1/4 = ₹15,000
Common mistake: ₹60,000 (A) is R's share for a full year (or the firm's profit for 3 months). Counting 4 months (April to July) gives ₹20,000 (B); counting 6 months gives ₹30,000 (C).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Death of a partner — accounting entry for share of profit
questions.question: When a deceased partner's share of profit from the date of the last balance sheet till the date of death is calculated on a time basis, it is recorded by debiting:
options: C) Profit and Loss Suspense Account
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Profit and Loss Suspense Account
Why: The firm's books are not closed on the date of death, so the actual profit for that part-year is not yet known. The estimated share is credited to the deceased partner's Capital Account and debited to a temporary 'Profit and Loss Suspense Account', which is closed when the year's accounts are prepared.
Why not the others:
(A) Revaluation Account records changes in the values of assets and liabilities.
(B) Realisation Account is opened only on dissolution of the firm.
(D) The deceased partner's Capital Account is CREDITED with his share, not debited.
Key point: Entry → Profit and Loss Suspense A/c Dr.; To Deceased Partner's Capital A/c.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.question: At the time of C's admission, the balance sheet of A and B (who share profits in the ratio 3 : 2) shows a General Reserve of ₹60,000. C is admitted for a 1/4th share. The amount of General Reserve credited to A's Capital Account will be:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹36,000
Given: General Reserve ₹60,000; old ratio of A and B 3 : 2.
Why this method: The reserve was built up from profits earned before C joined, so it belongs only to the old partners and is shared in the OLD ratio. C gets nothing from it.
Step 1: A's share = ₹60,000 × 3/5 = ₹36,000 (B's share = ₹24,000)
Common mistake: Giving C a share of the reserve and taking 3/4 of A's amount gives ₹27,000 (B). ₹45,000 (C) is 3/4 of the whole reserve. ₹24,000 (D) is B's share, not A's.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Retirement — amount due and Loan Account
questions.question: On X's retirement, the following balances relating to him were ascertained: Capital ₹1,20,000; share of goodwill ₹30,000; share of loss on revaluation ₹6,000; share of General Reserve ₹18,000. X was paid ₹62,000 in cash and the balance was transferred to his Loan Account. The amount transferred to X's Loan Account is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹1,00,000
Given: Capital ₹1,20,000; goodwill +₹30,000; revaluation loss −₹6,000; General Reserve +₹18,000; cash paid ₹62,000.
Step 1: Amount due = 1,20,000 + 30,000 − 6,000 + 18,000 = ₹1,62,000
Step 2: Balance transferred to Loan Account = ₹1,62,000 − ₹62,000 = ₹1,00,000
Common mistake: ₹1,62,000 (A) is the total due before the cash payment. Adding the revaluation loss instead of deducting it gives ₹1,74,000 − ₹62,000 = ₹1,12,000 (B). Leaving out the goodwill gives ₹1,32,000 − ₹62,000 = ₹70,000 (C).

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.question: The Realisation Account prepared at the time of dissolution of a partnership firm is a:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Nominal account
Why: The Realisation Account finds the profit or loss on selling the assets and settling the liabilities. Because it ends in a profit or loss that is transferred to the partners' capital accounts, it is a nominal account.
Why not the others:
(A) Real accounts record assets; the assets are only transferred into the Realisation Account.
(C) Personal accounts record persons, such as partners' capital accounts.
(D) A memorandum account is not part of the double-entry system, but the Realisation Account is.
Key point: Realisation Account → nominal; its balance = profit or loss on realisation, shared in the profit-sharing ratio.

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.question:
Under Section 48 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, arrange the following payments made out of the firm's assets on dissolution in the correct order:
(A) Amounts due to partners on account of capital
(B) Debts of the firm to third parties
(C) Loans and advances made by partners (other than capital)
(D) Residue, if any, divided among partners in their profit-sharing ratio
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (B), (C), (A), (D)
Why: Section 48(b) lays down the order in which the firm's assets (including contributions made to cover any deficiency) are applied:
1. Debts of the firm to third parties — outsiders are paid first → (B)
2. Advances made by partners, as distinct from capital → (C)
3. Amounts due to partners on account of capital → (A)
4. Any residue, divided in the profit-sharing ratio → (D)
Why not the others: (A) pays partners' loans before outsiders; (B) pays capital first; (D) pays capital before partners' loans.
Key point: Outsiders → partners' loans → partners' capital → surplus.

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.question: On dissolution of a firm: assets (other than cash) with a book value of ₹3,50,000 realised ₹3,10,000; creditors of ₹80,000 accepted ₹76,000 in full settlement; and realisation expenses of ₹5,000 were paid by the firm. The loss on realisation is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹41,000
Given: Assets ₹3,50,000 realised ₹3,10,000; creditors ₹80,000 settled at ₹76,000; expenses ₹5,000.
Step 1: Debit side of Realisation A/c = Assets ₹3,50,000 + Cash paid to creditors ₹76,000 + Expenses ₹5,000 = ₹4,31,000
Step 2: Credit side = Creditors transferred ₹80,000 + Cash from assets ₹3,10,000 = ₹3,90,000
Step 3: Loss = ₹4,31,000 − ₹3,90,000 = ₹41,000 (that is: loss on assets ₹40,000 − discount from creditors ₹4,000 + expenses ₹5,000)
Common mistake: Ignoring the creditors' discount gives ₹45,000 (B); ignoring the expenses gives ₹36,000 (C); treating the discount as a loss gives ₹49,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Accounts not transferred to the Realisation Account
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the dissolution of a partnership firm:
(A) A partner's loan to the firm is transferred to the Realisation Account.
(B) Partners' capital accounts are not transferred to the Realisation Account.
(C) Accumulated profits (General Reserve) are transferred to the partners' capital accounts in their profit-sharing ratio.
(D) Cash and bank balances are not transferred to the Realisation Account.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (B), (C) and (D) only
Why:
(A) False — a partner's loan is settled separately (by paying the partner through the Partner's Loan A/c), after outside liabilities and before capital.
(B) True — capital accounts are where the final settlement with partners takes place.
(C) True — reserves are undistributed profits of the partners, so they are credited to their capital accounts in the profit-sharing ratio.
(D) True — cash and bank are what the realisation produces, so they stay in the Cash/Bank Account.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) of the options include the false statement (A); (C) leaves out the true statement (B).
Key point: Realisation A/c takes assets (except cash, bank and fictitious assets) and outside liabilities only.

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Asset taken over and liability paid by a partner
questions.question: On dissolution, partner M takes over the firm's stock (book value ₹50,000) at ₹40,000 and agrees to pay a creditor of ₹20,000 personally. The net amount debited to M's Capital Account in respect of these two transactions is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹20,000
Given: Stock taken over at ₹40,000 (agreed value); creditor ₹20,000 paid by M personally.
Step 1: Asset taken over → M's Capital A/c Dr. ₹40,000; To Realisation A/c ₹40,000 (always at the agreed value, not the book value)
Step 2: Liability paid by the partner → Realisation A/c Dr. ₹20,000; To M's Capital A/c ₹20,000
Step 3: Net effect on M's Capital A/c = ₹40,000 debit − ₹20,000 credit = ₹20,000 net debit
Common mistake: Ignoring the creditor gives ₹40,000 (A); adding both amounts gives ₹60,000 (C); using the book value of stock gives ₹50,000 − ₹20,000 = ₹30,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Vardhan Ltd. invited applications for 40,000 equity shares of ₹10 each, issued at a premium of ₹2 per share. The amount was payable as follows: ₹5 on application (including the premium of ₹2), ₹3 on allotment, and ₹4 on the first and final call. Applications were received for 50,000 shares. Applications for 4,000 shares were rejected and the money was refunded. The remaining applicants were allotted shares on a pro-rata basis, and their excess application money was adjusted towards the amount due on allotment. Mohan, who had applied for 1,150 shares, failed to pay the allotment money and the call money. His shares were forfeited after the call. The forfeited shares were later re-issued at ₹8 per share as fully paid.

Question: The amount refunded to the applicants whose applications were rejected is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹20,000
Given: 4,000 shares rejected; application money ₹5 per share (including premium).
Step 1: Refund = 4,000 × ₹5 = ₹20,000 (the whole application money, premium included, is returned on rejected applications)
Common mistake: Using only the capital part of ₹3 gives ₹12,000 (A). ₹30,000 (B) is the excess money of the pro-rata applicants, which is adjusted against allotment, not refunded. ₹50,000 (D) treats all 10,000 excess shares as refunded.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Vardhan Ltd. invited applications for 40,000 equity shares of ₹10 each, issued at a premium of ₹2 per share. The amount was payable as follows: ₹5 on application (including the premium of ₹2), ₹3 on allotment, and ₹4 on the first and final call. Applications were received for 50,000 shares. Applications for 4,000 shares were rejected and the money was refunded. The remaining applicants were allotted shares on a pro-rata basis, and their excess application money was adjusted towards the amount due on allotment. Mohan, who had applied for 1,150 shares, failed to pay the allotment money and the call money. His shares were forfeited after the call. The forfeited shares were later re-issued at ₹8 per share as fully paid.

Question: The total excess application money adjusted towards allotment is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹30,000
Given: Pro-rata applicants applied for 50,000 − 4,000 = 46,000 shares and were allotted 40,000.
Step 1: Excess shares applied for = 46,000 − 40,000 = 6,000
Step 2: Excess money = 6,000 × ₹5 = ₹30,000, adjusted against allotment
Common mistake: ₹20,000 (B) is the refund on rejected applications. Using ₹3 per share instead of ₹5 gives ₹18,000 (C). ₹50,000 (D) wrongly uses all 10,000 excess shares.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Pro-rata allotment — calls in arrears on allotment
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Vardhan Ltd. invited applications for 40,000 equity shares of ₹10 each, issued at a premium of ₹2 per share. The amount was payable as follows: ₹5 on application (including the premium of ₹2), ₹3 on allotment, and ₹4 on the first and final call. Applications were received for 50,000 shares. Applications for 4,000 shares were rejected and the money was refunded. The remaining applicants were allotted shares on a pro-rata basis, and their excess application money was adjusted towards the amount due on allotment. Mohan, who had applied for 1,150 shares, failed to pay the allotment money and the call money. His shares were forfeited after the call. The forfeited shares were later re-issued at ₹8 per share as fully paid.

Question: The number of shares allotted to Mohan and the amount he failed to pay on allotment are:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 1,000 shares; ₹2,250
Given: Pro-rata ratio = 46,000 applied : 40,000 allotted = 23 : 20; Mohan applied for 1,150 shares.
Step 1: Shares allotted = 1,150 × 20/23 = 1,000
Step 2: Application money paid = 1,150 × ₹5 = ₹5,750; required for 1,000 shares = ₹5,000; excess = ₹750
Step 3: Allotment due = 1,000 × ₹3 = ₹3,000; less excess ₹750 = ₹2,250 unpaid
Common mistake: Allotting the full 1,150 shares gives (A). Forgetting the excess adjustment gives ₹3,000 (B). Valuing the excess at ₹3 per share (150 × ₹3 = ₹450) gives ₹2,550 (C).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Vardhan Ltd. invited applications for 40,000 equity shares of ₹10 each, issued at a premium of ₹2 per share. The amount was payable as follows: ₹5 on application (including the premium of ₹2), ₹3 on allotment, and ₹4 on the first and final call. Applications were received for 50,000 shares. Applications for 4,000 shares were rejected and the money was refunded. The remaining applicants were allotted shares on a pro-rata basis, and their excess application money was adjusted towards the amount due on allotment. Mohan, who had applied for 1,150 shares, failed to pay the allotment money and the call money. His shares were forfeited after the call. The forfeited shares were later re-issued at ₹8 per share as fully paid.

Question: On forfeiture of Mohan's shares, the amount credited to the Share Forfeiture Account is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹3,750
Given: 1,000 shares fully called up (₹10 each); unpaid allotment ₹2,250; unpaid call 1,000 × ₹4 = ₹4,000. The premium was received with the application money, so Securities Premium is not touched.
Formula: Share Forfeiture = Called-up capital − Calls unpaid (= capital money actually received)
Step 1: Share Capital A/c Dr. = 1,000 × ₹10 = ₹10,000
Step 2: Calls unpaid = ₹2,250 + ₹4,000 = ₹6,250
Step 3: Share Forfeiture A/c Cr. = ₹10,000 − ₹6,250 = ₹3,750 (application ₹3,000 towards capital + excess ₹750 adjusted on allotment)
Common mistake: ₹5,750 (A) includes the ₹2,000 premium, which is not forfeited. ₹3,000 (D) ignores the excess ₹750 adjusted on allotment. ₹1,750 (C) is the capital reserve after re-issue.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Re-issue of forfeited shares — capital reserve
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Vardhan Ltd. invited applications for 40,000 equity shares of ₹10 each, issued at a premium of ₹2 per share. The amount was payable as follows: ₹5 on application (including the premium of ₹2), ₹3 on allotment, and ₹4 on the first and final call. Applications were received for 50,000 shares. Applications for 4,000 shares were rejected and the money was refunded. The remaining applicants were allotted shares on a pro-rata basis, and their excess application money was adjusted towards the amount due on allotment. Mohan, who had applied for 1,150 shares, failed to pay the allotment money and the call money. His shares were forfeited after the call. The forfeited shares were later re-issued at ₹8 per share as fully paid.

Question: After the re-issue of the forfeited shares, the amount transferred to Capital Reserve is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹1,750
Given: Forfeited amount on 1,000 shares = ₹3,750; re-issued at ₹8 as fully paid (₹10 face value), so the discount is ₹2 per share.
Step 1: Discount on re-issue = 1,000 × ₹2 = ₹2,000, debited to Share Forfeiture A/c
Step 2: Balance in Share Forfeiture A/c = ₹3,750 − ₹2,000 = ₹1,750
Step 3: This balance is a capital profit → Share Forfeiture A/c Dr. ₹1,750; To Capital Reserve A/c ₹1,750
Common mistake: Transferring the whole forfeited amount gives ₹3,750 (A). ₹2,000 (B) is the discount on re-issue. Deducting the unpaid allotment of ₹2,250 instead of the discount gives ₹1,500 (D).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Issue of securities at a discount
questions.question: Under the Companies Act, 2013, which of the following can a company issue at a discount in the normal course?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Debentures
Why: Section 53 of the Companies Act, 2013 prohibits a company from issuing shares at a discount (the only exception is sweat equity shares). Debentures are a form of borrowing and may be issued at par, at a premium or at a discount.
Why not the others:
(A) and (B) Equity and preference shares cannot be issued at a discount — such an issue is void.
(C) Bonus shares are issued free to existing shareholders as fully paid, so the question of a discount does not arise.
Key point: Shares → par or premium only; debentures → par, premium or discount.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.question: A company issued 5,000, 9% debentures of ₹100 each at a discount of 5%, redeemable at a premium of 10% after five years. The total loss on issue of debentures is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹75,000
Given: 5,000 debentures of ₹100; issued at 5% discount; redeemable at 10% premium.
Formula: Loss on issue = Discount on issue + Premium on redemption
Step 1: Discount on issue = 5,000 × ₹5 = ₹25,000
Step 2: Premium on redemption = 5,000 × ₹10 = ₹50,000 (credited to Premium on Redemption of Debentures A/c, a liability)
Step 3: Loss on issue = ₹25,000 + ₹50,000 = ₹75,000
Common mistake: ₹25,000 (B) counts only the discount; ₹50,000 (C) counts only the redemption premium; ₹1,00,000 (D) uses 20% instead of 15%.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Presentation of share capital and debentures in the balance sheet
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II with reference to the balance sheet of a company prepared as per Schedule III:

List-I (Item)
(A) Calls in arrears
(B) Securities Premium
(C) 10% Debentures redeemable after 5 years
(D) Interest accrued and due on debentures

List-II (Presentation)
(I) Long-term borrowings
(II) Other current liabilities
(III) Deducted from subscribed capital under 'Share Capital'
(IV) Reserves and Surplus

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Why:
(A) Calls in arrears are shown as a deduction from 'Subscribed but not fully paid' capital in the notes to Share Capital → (III).
(B) Securities Premium is a capital reserve shown under Reserves and Surplus → (IV).
(C) Debentures repayable after more than 12 months are Long-term borrowings → (I).
(D) Interest that has accrued and fallen due is payable within the year → Other current liabilities → (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps calls in arrears and securities premium; (B) swaps the two debenture items; (D) treats calls in arrears as a liability.
Key point: Long-term debt → non-current liabilities; interest due on it → current liabilities.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.question:
Securities Premium can be used by a company for which of the following purposes?
(A) Issuing fully paid bonus shares to its members
(B) Paying dividend to shareholders
(C) Writing off discount allowed on the issue of debentures
(D) Buying back its own shares
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (C) and (D) only
Why: Section 52(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 allows Securities Premium to be used only for: issuing fully paid bonus shares; writing off preliminary expenses; writing off expenses of, commission paid on, or discount allowed on any issue of shares or debentures; providing for the premium payable on redemption of preference shares or debentures; and buying back its own shares.
Why not the others: Paying dividend (statement B) is NOT a permitted use — Securities Premium is a capital receipt and cannot be distributed as dividend. Options (A), (C) and (D) all include statement (B).
Key point: Securities Premium → capital purposes only, never dividend.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Issue of shares for consideration other than cash
questions.question: Kiran Ltd. purchased assets worth ₹4,40,000 from Sona Traders. The purchase consideration was paid by issuing equity shares of ₹100 each at a premium of 10%. The number of shares issued is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 4,000
Given: Purchase consideration ₹4,40,000; issue price = ₹100 + 10% premium = ₹110 per share.
Formula: Number of shares = Purchase consideration ÷ Issue price
Step 1: Number of shares = ₹4,40,000 ÷ ₹110 = 4,000 shares (Share Capital ₹4,00,000 + Securities Premium ₹40,000)
Common mistake: Dividing by the face value of ₹100 gives 4,400 (A). Multiplying instead of dividing gives 4,840 (B). Treating the premium as a discount gives 3,600 (C).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.question: A shareholder holding 2,000 shares failed to pay the final call of ₹4 per share due on 1 October 2025 and paid it on 31 December 2025. The company has adopted Table F. The interest charged on calls in arrears is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹200
Given: Arrears = 2,000 × ₹4 = ₹8,000; delay = 1 October to 31 December = 3 months; Table F rate on calls in arrears = 10% p.a.
Step 1: Interest = ₹8,000 × 10/100 × 3/12 = ₹200
Common mistake: Using the Table F rate for calls in ADVANCE (12% p.a.) gives ₹240 (B). Charging for a full year gives ₹800 (C). Counting 4 months gives ₹267 (D).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.question: Leela Ltd. issued ₹5,00,000, 10% debentures on 1 July 2025. The company closes its books on 31 March every year. The interest on debentures for the year 2025-26 is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹37,500
Given: Debentures ₹5,00,000 @ 10% p.a.; outstanding from 1 July 2025 to 31 March 2026 = 9 months.
Step 1: Interest = ₹5,00,000 × 10/100 × 9/12 = ₹37,500 (a charge against profit, debited to the Statement of Profit and Loss)
Common mistake: Charging a full year gives ₹50,000 (A); 6 months gives ₹25,000 (C); 10 months gives ₹41,667 (D).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.question:
Assertion (A): Debentures issued as collateral security may be shown in the balance sheet by way of a note below the loan for which they have been issued.
Reason (R): Interest is payable on debentures issued as collateral security from the date of their issue.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
Why: Collateral debentures are issued only as secondary security for a loan. They may be shown either by a note below the loan (first method) or by recording them and deducting 'Debentures Suspense A/c' (second method), so the Assertion is true. The Reason is false: no interest is payable on collateral debentures — interest is paid only on the actual loan. The debentures become a real liability only if the lender enforces them on default.
Why not the others:
(A) and (B) need the Reason to be true.
(D) The Assertion correctly states one of the two accepted methods.
Key point: Collateral debentures → no cash received, no interest, no extra liability unless the security is enforced.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Financial statements of a company — Schedule III headings
questions.question: As per Schedule III of the Companies Act, 2013, 'Bills Payable' are shown in the balance sheet of a company under:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Trade payables
Why: Trade payables are amounts owed to suppliers for goods and services bought in the normal course of business. They include both creditors and bills payable, and are shown under Current Liabilities.
Why not the others:
(B) Short-term borrowings are loans repayable within 12 months, such as a bank overdraft.
(C) Other current liabilities include items like unpaid dividends, interest accrued and calls in advance.
(D) Short-term provisions include the provision for tax and similar items.
Key point: Creditors + Bills Payable = Trade Payables.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Tools of financial analysis — common-size statements
questions.question: In a common-size Statement of Profit and Loss, each item is expressed as a percentage of:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Revenue from operations
Why: A common-size statement converts every figure into a percentage of a common base so that firms or years can be compared. For the Statement of Profit and Loss the base is Revenue from operations (= 100). For the balance sheet the base is total assets (or total of equity and liabilities).
Why not the others:
(A) Net profit is itself one of the items being expressed.
(B) Total assets is the base for a common-size balance sheet.
(D) Shareholders' funds is never used as the base.
Key point: Income statement base = Revenue from operations; balance sheet base = Total assets.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.question: A company's current assets are ₹3,00,000, which include inventory of ₹60,000 and prepaid expenses of ₹15,000. Its current liabilities are ₹1,50,000. The quick ratio is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 1.5 : 1
Given: Current assets ₹3,00,000; inventory ₹60,000; prepaid expenses ₹15,000; current liabilities ₹1,50,000.
Formula: Quick ratio = Quick assets ÷ Current liabilities, where Quick assets = Current assets − Inventory − Prepaid expenses
Step 1: Quick assets = ₹3,00,000 − ₹60,000 − ₹15,000 = ₹2,25,000
Step 2: Quick ratio = ₹2,25,000 ÷ ₹1,50,000 = 1.5 : 1
Common mistake: Deducting only the inventory gives 1.6 : 1 (A); 2 : 1 (C) is the current ratio; deducting only the prepaid expenses gives 1.9 : 1 (D).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Ratio)
(A) Interest coverage ratio
(B) Trade receivables turnover ratio
(C) Current ratio
(D) Return on investment

List-II (Type of ratio)
(I) Profitability ratio
(II) Liquidity ratio
(III) Solvency ratio
(IV) Activity ratio

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Why:
(A) Interest coverage measures the ability to pay interest on long-term debt → solvency (III).
(B) Trade receivables turnover measures how fast receivables are collected → activity (IV).
(C) Current ratio measures short-term debt-paying ability → liquidity (II).
(D) Return on investment measures the return earned on capital employed → profitability (I).
Why not the others: (A) swaps the liquidity and solvency ratios; (B) swaps the activity and liquidity ratios; (C) swaps the solvency and profitability ratios.
Key point: Liquidity = short-term; solvency = long-term; activity = speed of use; profitability = return.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Cash flow statement — classification of activities
questions.question:
For a non-financial company, consider the following statements about the cash flow statement prepared as per AS-3 (Revised):
(A) Interest paid on debentures is a financing activity.
(B) Dividend received on investments is an investing activity.
(C) Purchase of machinery is an investing activity.
(D) Income tax paid on operating profit is a financing activity.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why:
(A) True — interest paid is a cost of raising funds, so for a non-financial company it is a financing outflow.
(B) True — dividend received is a return on investments → investing inflow.
(C) True — buying a non-current asset is an investing outflow.
(D) False — income tax paid is normally classified under operating activities, unless it can be specifically identified with financing or investing activities.
Why not the others: Options (A), (B) and (D) all include the false statement (D).
Key point: Non-financial company → interest/dividend PAID = financing; interest/dividend RECEIVED = investing; tax = operating.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.question: From the following information, calculate the debt-equity ratio: Long-term borrowings ₹4,00,000; Equity share capital ₹3,00,000; Reserves and surplus ₹2,00,000.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 0.8 : 1
Given: Debt (long-term borrowings) ₹4,00,000; Equity (shareholders' funds) = ₹3,00,000 + ₹2,00,000 = ₹5,00,000.
Formula: Debt-equity ratio = Long-term debts ÷ Shareholders' funds
Step 1: Ratio = ₹4,00,000 ÷ ₹5,00,000 = 0.8 : 1
Common mistake: Leaving out reserves gives ₹4,00,000 ÷ ₹3,00,000 = 1.33 : 1 (B). Inverting the ratio gives 1.25 : 1 (C). Dividing debt by (debt + equity) gives 0.44 : 1 (D), which is a different ratio.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.question: Revenue from operations is ₹8,00,000 and the gross profit is 25% of revenue from operations. Opening inventory is ₹90,000 and closing inventory is ₹1,10,000. The inventory turnover ratio is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 6 times
Given: Revenue ₹8,00,000; GP 25% of revenue; opening inventory ₹90,000; closing inventory ₹1,10,000.
Formula: Inventory turnover ratio = Cost of revenue from operations ÷ Average inventory
Step 1: Gross profit = 25% × ₹8,00,000 = ₹2,00,000; Cost of revenue = ₹8,00,000 − ₹2,00,000 = ₹6,00,000
Step 2: Average inventory = (₹90,000 + ₹1,10,000) ÷ 2 = ₹1,00,000
Step 3: Ratio = ₹6,00,000 ÷ ₹1,00,000 = 6 times
Common mistake: Using revenue instead of cost gives 8 times (A). Revenue ÷ closing inventory gives 7.27 times (B). Cost ÷ closing inventory gives 5.45 times (C).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Cash flow from operating activities — indirect method
questions.question: Net profit before tax is ₹2,00,000. Depreciation charged is ₹30,000; profit on sale of machinery is ₹10,000; trade receivables increased by ₹25,000; and trade payables increased by ₹15,000. Cash generated from operations (before tax) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹2,10,000
Given: NPBT ₹2,00,000; depreciation ₹30,000 (non-cash); profit on sale of machinery ₹10,000 (investing item); receivables +₹25,000; payables +₹15,000.
Step 1: Operating profit before working-capital changes = 2,00,000 + 30,000 − 10,000 = ₹2,20,000
Step 2: Less increase in trade receivables (cash tied up) = −₹25,000
Step 3: Add increase in trade payables (cash retained) = +₹15,000
Step 4: Cash generated from operations = 2,20,000 − 25,000 + 15,000 = ₹2,10,000
Common mistake: Adding back the profit on sale instead of deducting it gives ₹2,30,000 (A). Ignoring working-capital changes gives ₹2,20,000 (C). Treating the increase in payables as an outflow gives ₹1,80,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Cash flow from investing activities — machinery account
questions.question: Machinery (net of depreciation) was ₹5,00,000 at the beginning of the year and ₹6,00,000 at the end. Depreciation charged during the year was ₹70,000. Machinery with a book value of ₹40,000 was sold for ₹35,000. Net cash used in investing activities in respect of machinery is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹1,75,000
Given: Opening ₹5,00,000; closing ₹6,00,000; depreciation ₹70,000; book value sold ₹40,000; sale proceeds ₹35,000.
Formula: Purchase = Closing balance + Depreciation + Book value of machinery sold − Opening balance
Step 1: Purchase = 6,00,000 + 70,000 + 40,000 − 5,00,000 = ₹2,10,000 (outflow)
Step 2: Sale proceeds = ₹35,000 (inflow; the loss of ₹5,000 is adjusted in operating activities)
Step 3: Net cash used = ₹2,10,000 − ₹35,000 = ₹1,75,000
Common mistake: ₹2,10,000 (B) shows only the purchase. Taking the book value of ₹40,000 as the sale proceeds gives ₹1,70,000 (C). Ignoring depreciation when finding the purchase gives ₹1,40,000 − ₹35,000 = ₹1,05,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Liquidity ratios — effect of a transaction on current ratio
questions.question: A company's current ratio is 2.5 : 1 and its working capital is ₹1,80,000. If it now pays a trade creditor ₹20,000 in cash, its new current ratio will be:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 2.8 : 1
Given: CA : CL = 2.5 : 1; working capital (CA − CL) = ₹1,80,000.
Step 1: CA − CL = 2.5 CL − CL = 1.5 CL = ₹1,80,000 → CL = ₹1,20,000; CA = ₹3,00,000
Step 2: Paying a creditor reduces BOTH: CA = ₹3,00,000 − ₹20,000 = ₹2,80,000; CL = ₹1,20,000 − ₹20,000 = ₹1,00,000
Step 3: New current ratio = ₹2,80,000 ÷ ₹1,00,000 = 2.8 : 1
Common mistake: Assuming the ratio is unchanged gives (A). Reducing only current assets gives 2,80,000 ÷ 1,20,000 = 2.33 : 1 (B). (D) comes from an arithmetic slip. Remember: when the ratio is above 1, paying a current liability increases it.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Structure of CAS — codification and hierarchy of account heads
questions.question: In a computerised accounting system, giving every account a unique code so that accounts are grouped into a hierarchy (for example, 1000 Assets → 1100 Current Assets → 1110 Cash) is known as:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Codification of accounts
Why: Codification assigns structured numeric or alphanumeric codes to account heads, following the chart of accounts. Each level of the code shows a group, sub-group and ledger account, so the software can sort, retrieve and summarise data quickly.
Why not the others:
(A) Data validation checks that input data is correct and complete.
(C) Back-up is a copy of data kept for safety.
(D) An audit trail is a record that traces each transaction to its source.
Key point: Chart of accounts + codification = the hierarchy of account heads in CAS.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.question: Which spreadsheet function calculates depreciation under the straight-line method?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) =SLN()
Why: SLN(cost, salvage, life) returns the equal yearly depreciation under the straight-line method, i.e. (cost − salvage) ÷ life.
Why not the others:
(A) PMT calculates the periodic instalment of a loan.
(B) DDB calculates depreciation under the double-declining balance (written-down) method.
(C) NPV calculates the net present value of future cash flows.
Key point: SLN = straight line; DDB = double declining; PMT = loan instalment.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.question: A machine is purchased for ₹1,10,000. Its estimated salvage value is ₹10,000 and its useful life is 5 years. The value returned by =SLN(110000,10000,5) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 20,000
Given: Cost 1,10,000; salvage 10,000; life 5 years.
Formula: SLN = (Cost − Salvage) ÷ Life
Step 1: (1,10,000 − 10,000) ÷ 5 = 1,00,000 ÷ 5 = 20,000 per year
Common mistake: Ignoring the salvage value gives 22,000 (B). Deducting the salvage twice gives 18,000 (C). Adding the salvage instead of deducting it gives 24,000 (D).

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Types of computerised accounting systems and AIS
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(A) Ready-to-use accounting software
(B) Customised accounting software
(C) Tailor-made accounting software
(D) Accounting Information System (AIS)

List-II
(I) Developed specially to meet the unique requirements of a large organisation
(II) A standard package modified to suit the specific needs of the user
(III) A low-cost standard package suitable for small businesses with few transactions
(IV) A system that collects, stores and processes financial data to provide information to decision-makers

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(III), (B)-(II), (C)-(I), (D)-(IV)
Why:
(A) Ready-to-use software is a low-cost, standard package with little training needed — suited to small businesses → (III).
(B) Customised software is a standard package adapted to the user's special needs → (II).
(C) Tailor-made software is built from scratch for a large organisation's unique needs → (I).
(D) An AIS collects, stores and processes accounting data to give useful information → (IV).
Why not the others: (A) reverses ready-to-use and tailor-made; (B) swaps customised and tailor-made; (D) swaps ready-to-use and customised.
Key point: Ready-to-use → customised → tailor-made means rising cost, rising flexibility and rising organisation size.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about a computerised accounting system:
(A) It processes large volumes of transactions faster than a manual system.
(B) It removes the need for any internal control.
(C) Reports such as the trial balance can be generated instantly.
(D) Data may be lost if a regular back-up is not maintained.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (C) and (D) only
Why:
(A) True — speed is a key advantage of CAS.
(B) False — CAS still needs internal controls such as passwords, access rights, authorisation and audit trails, to prevent errors and fraud.
(C) True — once entries are made, reports are generated automatically and instantly.
(D) True — system failure, viruses or hardware damage can destroy data, so back-ups are essential (a limitation of CAS).
Why not the others: Options (A), (B) and (C) all include the false statement (B).
Key point: CAS is fast and accurate, but it depends on controls and back-ups.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Electronic spreadsheet — relative and absolute cell references
questions.question: Cell D2 of a spreadsheet contains the formula =B2*$C$1. If this formula is copied to cell D3, it will become:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) =B3*$C$1
Why: B2 is a RELATIVE reference, so when the formula moves one row down, it changes to B3. $C$1 is an ABSOLUTE reference — the $ signs lock both the column and the row — so it stays as $C$1. This is how a fixed rate (such as a tax rate in C1) is applied to a whole column of values.
Why not the others:
(A) The relative reference would not stay as B2.
(C) The absolute reference $C$1 cannot change to $C$2.
(D) Copying down a column does not change the column letters.
Key point: $ locks a reference; references without $ adjust when copied.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.question: A pivot table in a spreadsheet is mainly used to:
options: A) Protect a worksheet with a password
B) Check formulas for spelling errors
C) Summarise and analyse large data by grouping it
D) Convert a worksheet into a PDF file
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Summarise and analyse large data by grouping it
Why: A pivot table quickly groups, totals, counts and averages large data sets — for example, total sales by region and month — without writing formulas. This makes it useful for preparing accounting reports.
Why not the others:
(A) Password protection is a sheet- or workbook-protection feature.
(B) Spelling checks are done with the spell-check tool.
(D) PDF conversion is done with the Save As/Export option.
Key point: Pivot table = fast summary report from raw data.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.question: A loan of ₹1,00,000 is to be repaid in 2 equal annual instalments at an interest rate of 10% p.a., each instalment being paid at the end of the year. The instalment returned by =PMT(10%,2,-100000) is closest to:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹57,619
Given: Principal ₹1,00,000; rate 10% p.a.; 2 annual payments at the end of each year.
Formula: Instalment = P × r ÷ [1 − (1 + r)^(−n)]
Step 1: (1.10)^(−2) = 1 ÷ 1.21 = 0.826446
Step 2: 1 − 0.826446 = 0.173554
Step 3: Instalment = 1,00,000 × 0.10 ÷ 0.173554 ≈ ₹57,619
Check: Year 1 interest ₹10,000, principal repaid ₹47,619, balance ₹52,381; Year 2 interest ₹5,238 + principal ₹52,381 = ₹57,619 ✔
Common mistake: ₹55,000 (B) adds simple average interest to equal principal. ₹60,500 (C) splits the compound amount ₹1,21,000 in two. ₹50,000 (D) ignores interest altogether.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.question: Which error value does a spreadsheet display when a formula refers to a cell that has been deleted?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) #REF!
Why: #REF! means the formula has an invalid cell reference — usually because a referenced row, column or cell was deleted, or the formula was pasted where its references no longer exist.
Why not the others:
(A) #VALUE! appears when the wrong type of data is used, for example adding text to a number.
(B) #NAME? appears when Excel does not recognise a function or range name, such as a misspelt function.
(C) #DIV/0! appears when a number is divided by zero or by an empty cell.
Key point: Deleted reference → #REF!; wrong data type → #VALUE!; unknown name → #NAME?; division by zero → #DIV/0!.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.question: In a payroll spreadsheet, an employee's basic pay is ₹40,000. Dearness Allowance (DA) is 50% of basic pay; House Rent Allowance (HRA) is 20% of (basic pay + DA); and the Provident Fund (PF) deduction is 12% of (basic pay + DA). The employee's net salary is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹64,800
Given: Basic ₹40,000; DA 50% of basic; HRA 20% of (basic + DA); PF 12% of (basic + DA).
Step 1: DA = 50% × ₹40,000 = ₹20,000; Basic + DA = ₹60,000
Step 2: HRA = 20% × ₹60,000 = ₹12,000
Step 3: Gross salary = ₹40,000 + ₹20,000 + ₹12,000 = ₹72,000
Step 4: PF = 12% × ₹60,000 = ₹7,200
Step 5: Net salary = ₹72,000 − ₹7,200 = ₹64,800
Common mistake: ₹72,000 (A) is the gross salary before the PF deduction. Calculating PF on basic pay only (₹4,800) gives ₹67,200 (C). ₹60,000 (D) leaves out both HRA and PF.
